title: Tropical cyclone passage did not change shallow earthquake rates within 200 km in global ComCat (M4.5+, 1980-2026) and Japan JMA (M2.5+, 1998-2024) catalogs
abstract: Question: do tropical cyclones change the rate of shallow earthquakes near their tracks? Earlier studies report typhoon-triggered slow slip in Taiwan and propose pressure unloading or rain loading. Approach: we compared earthquake counts near 4,100 IBTrACS storm tracks (1980-2026; global USGS ComCat, M 4.5 or more) and near 383 storms close to Japan (1998-2024; JMA catalog, M 2.5 or more) with counts for the same tracks and calendar dates moved by 1 to 6 years. We removed aftershocks (Gardner-Knopoff), used a season bootstrap for intervals and a season label test for p-values. Result: for shallow events (30 km or less) within 200 km, the rate ratio in the passage window (-1 to +1 day) was 1.01 (95% CI 0.76-1.30) globally and 1.01 (0.86-1.15) in Japan. After the passage it was 1.04 (0.88-1.19) and 1.07 (1.01-1.13, label-test p 0.10, Holm p 0.58) for +1 to +10 days, and 0.99 and 1.01 for +10 to +60 days. Land events, events near the track, strong storms and large local pressure drops did not show a larger effect. Deep events (a control) and small Japanese events (no storm-noise detection loss) gave ratios near 1. A global excess 1 to 3 days before closest approach (ratio 1.45, not pre-specified) comes from coincidences such as the 2021 Kermadec M 8.1 sequence before Cyclone Niran. Limitations: high magnitude thresholds, few global land events, no rainfall data, residual aftershocks of very large earthquakes, and no test of slow slip or of effects longer than 60 days.
